history.note: AI-written draft of the capstone guide and rubric. Not yet reviewed by a human.

Comprehensive audit: criterion-specific level 2 and 3 descriptions, level 4 descriptions that cover everything level 3 lacks, level 1 communication text consistent with the required reflection, one rule for unverified numbers in the evidence criterion and step 3, clearer guidance for steps 1 and 2. Steps, fields, weights, and completion rules unchanged. Rubric still provisional. Not reviewed or approved by a human.

title: SDG Economic Challenge Capstone
intro: In this self-directed project, you pick one UN Sustainable Development Goal (SDG), define a problem through an economist's eyes, and propose a realistic solution.
This isn't a graded assignment. It's a project you complete on your own. Use the rubric to check your work, and ask the AI coach questions if you want.
Submitting it does not count as an official academic grade or certification.

steps.title: 1. Choose an SDG
steps.guidance: Pick one SDG that interests you and write why you chose it. If you can, name the specific target your problem affects (for example, target 6.1).

fields.label: Why you chose this SDG
fields.help: Connect it to your own experience or interests.

steps.title: 2. Define the economic problem
steps.guidance: Be specific: whose problem is it, and what scarcity or choice is involved? Narrowing it to one place or one market helps. Leave your solution for step 6.

fields.label: Problem definition
fields.help: What is the problem, and why is it an economic problem?

steps.title: 3. Economic concepts and evidence
steps.guidance: Write down the economic concepts that explain the problem (supply and demand, externalities, opportunity cost, etc.) and the evidence you checked yourself. When you use numbers, include the source (title, publisher, date). Use only numbers you checked in a source, or estimates and assumptions that you clearly label as such; flag any claim you could not verify.

fields.label: Related economic concepts
fields.help: Name each concept and explain how it works in this problem.

fields.label: Evidence and sources
fields.help: Title, publisher, and date of each source you checked yourself. Label any estimate or assumption, and flag any claim you could not verify.

steps.title: 4. Stakeholders
steps.guidance: List the people and groups affected by this problem and where each one stands.

fields.label: Stakeholders and their positions
fields.help: Consumers, producers, government, future generations, etc.

steps.title: 5. Incentives and trade-offs
steps.guidance: Describe the incentives (gains and costs) each stakeholder responds to and the trade-offs involved.

fields.label: Incentives and trade-offs
fields.help: Choices between efficiency and equity, now and the future, costs and benefits

steps.title: 6. Propose a solution
steps.guidance: Propose a realistic solution (a policy, an institution, or a change in behavior) and compare it with other options.

fields.label: Solution and comparison with alternatives
fields.help: Your proposed approach and the alternatives you compared it with

steps.title: 7. Evaluate costs, benefits, and limits
steps.guidance: Write down the expected costs and benefits of your solution, who pays, and its limits and uncertainties.

fields.label: Costs, benefits, and limits
fields.help: Who gains and who pays? What assumptions does it rely on?

steps.title: 8. Final proposal
steps.guidance: Using your earlier steps, write a proposal that a reader can easily follow.

fields.label: Final proposal
fields.help: In this order: problem → evidence → solution → costs and benefits → limits

steps.title: 9. Reflect
steps.guidance: Write what you learned, what changed your mind, and what you want to explore further.

fields.label: Reflection
fields.help: What did you learn, and what would you do differently next time?

rubric.note: These are suggested criteria and weights. They are provisional until a human (platform admin) reviews them, and they are a self-check tool, not an official score.

criteria.name: Accuracy of economic concepts
criteria.description: Are economic concepts used correctly and applied to the problem?

descriptors.1: Concepts are missing or used incorrectly.
descriptors.2: Names relevant concepts, but some are used incorrectly or only named, not applied to the problem.
descriptors.3: Uses the main concepts correctly and applies each to the problem, but does not fully explain how they produce it.
descriptors.4: Uses concepts correctly and explains how they produce the problem (the mechanism).

criteria.name: Problem definition
criteria.description: Is the scope clear, and is it framed as an economic problem?

descriptors.2: Names a problem, but who is affected, where, or the economic cause is missing or unclear.
descriptors.3: States who is affected, where, and an economic cause, but the scope is still broad or there is no measure of the problem.
descriptors.4: The scope, the people affected, how the problem is measured, and the causes are clear.

criteria.name: Quality of evidence
criteria.description: Does it give checked evidence and sources, label estimates and assumptions, and flag claims that could not be verified?

descriptors.1: There is no evidence or source.
descriptors.2: Gives some evidence, but sources are incomplete (missing title, publisher, or date), or unchecked numbers are not labeled as estimates.
descriptors.3: Supports the key claims with checked sources (title, publisher, date) and labels any estimates, but does not discuss the limits of the evidence.
descriptors.4: Uses clearly sourced evidence, labels estimates and assumptions, and states the limits of the evidence.

criteria.name: Stakeholder analysis
criteria.description: Does it cover the affected groups and their positions?

descriptors.2: Names several groups, but their positions and interests are missing or one-sided.
descriptors.3: Describes the positions of the main groups, but leaves out an important group (such as people with no voice in the market) or treats some only briefly.
descriptors.4: Gives balanced attention to the positions and interests of several groups, including groups with no voice in the market.

criteria.name: Incentives and trade-offs
criteria.description: Are incentives and trade-offs explained in economic terms?

descriptors.2: Mentions incentives or trade-offs, but does not explain them in terms of gains and costs.
descriptors.3: Explains the main incentives and at least one trade-off in terms of gains and costs, but misses some stakeholders or trade-offs.
descriptors.4: Clearly explains the key trade-offs and incentives for each main stakeholder, in terms of gains and costs.

criteria.name: Feasibility of the solution
criteria.description: Does it propose a realistic solution after weighing costs, benefits, and limits?

descriptors.1: The solution is unrealistic or not evaluated.
descriptors.2: Proposes a solution, but its costs and benefits are missing or it is not compared with any alternative.
descriptors.3: Compares the solution with at least one alternative on costs and benefits, but does not address funding, limits, or uncertainty.
descriptors.4: Weighs costs, benefits, and limits against alternatives, including funding and uncertainty.

criteria.name: Connection to the SDG
criteria.description: Are the problem and solution clearly linked to the chosen SDG?

descriptors.1: The link to the SDG is weak.
descriptors.2: Names an SDG, but the link to the problem or the solution is only general.
descriptors.3: Clearly links the problem and the solution to the chosen SDG, but not to a specific target or indicator.
descriptors.4: Explains the link at the level of a specific SDG target and indicator.

criteria.name: Communication and reflection
criteria.description: Is the proposal easy to read, and does it reflect on what was learned?

descriptors.1: Disorganized, and the reflection does not say what was learned.
descriptors.2: Some parts are out of order or hard to follow, and the reflection stays general.
descriptors.3: Mostly follows the order problem → evidence → solution → costs and benefits → limits, and the reflection names a limitation but no clear next step.
descriptors.4: Logically organized in that order, with a specific reflection on limitations and next steps.
